SQL MIGRATION LOCK CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Will this migration take your database down?

Almost every migration that causes an outage looks completely routine in review. The statement itself takes milliseconds — but it needs a lock that conflicts with ordinary reads, and if anything is still running on that table it waits, with every later query queued behind it. Paste your PostgreSQL migration below.

Nothing is uploaded. The SQL you paste is parsed in this browser and never leaves your device; this tool makes no network calls and never connects to a database.

1. Paste your migration

One migration file, or several concatenated. Comments, dollar-quoted function bodies and BEGIN/COMMIT blocks are all handled — and the transaction blocks matter, because three of the checks are about what shares a transaction with what.

Paste a migration above and click Check.

Findings

Prefer a CLI, or want this as a CI gate?

Same engine, zero dependencies, no database connection:

node check.mjs                     # scan every .sql under the current directory
node check.mjs db/migrate          # scan one directory or one file
node check.mjs --format json       # machine-readable
node check.mjs --list-checks       # exactly what is checked, and at what severity
node check.mjs --fail-on-risk      # exit 2 if a statement can block the table

Save the three files this page itself runs on — check.mjs, engine.mjs and sql.mjs — into one directory. Node's standard library only, nothing to install, no network calls, no connection string. Wiring --fail-on-risk into CI is the point: it catches the CREATE INDEX that someone added without CONCURRENTLY while the migration is still a pull request, which is the only moment fixing it is free.

What it checks

The whole list — there is nothing hidden behind it. The three marked relational are the ones a per-statement linter cannot make, because the answer depends on another statement in the file.

    Common questions

    My migration is one line and takes milliseconds. How can it cause an outage?

    Because the time a statement takes to run and the time it takes to start are different numbers. An ALTER TABLE needs an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, which conflicts with every other lock — including the ACCESS SHARE that a plain SELECT holds. If any query is still running on that table when your migration arrives, the migration waits. While it waits it sits at the head of the lock queue, and every query arriving after it queues behind it, because PostgreSQL will not let a weaker lock jump ahead of a stronger one that is already waiting. So one slow analytics SELECT, a forgotten open transaction, or a pg_dump is enough to make the table unavailable to everyone for as long as that query runs. SET lock_timeout = '3s' converts that from an outage into a migration that fails and can be retried.

    Isn't ADD COLUMN with a DEFAULT safe now?

    With a constant default, yes — since PostgreSQL 11 that is a metadata-only change, and this tool does not flag it. The exception is a VOLATILE default, which has to be evaluated separately for every existing row and therefore rewrites the whole table under an exclusive lock. gen_random_uuid() and random() are volatile; now() and CURRENT_TIMESTAMP are STABLE and are not. The two statements look nearly identical, which is exactly why this is worth a checker rather than a habit.

    Why does SET NOT NULL get flagged when it changes no data?

    Because it has to prove no existing row is null, and it does that with a full table scan while holding an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock — so reads and writes both block for the length of the scan. PostgreSQL 12 and later have a fast path: if a validated CHECK constraint already proves the column is not null, the scan is skipped. This tool reads the rest of your file to see whether you took that path, and stays quiet if you did. That is a fact about the file rather than about the statement, which is why a per-statement linter cannot tell the two apart.

    Does a clean result mean the migration is safe to run?

    No. This checks a specific, named list of statement-level patterns — the whole list is on this page and behind --list-checks, and there is nothing hidden. It cannot see how large your tables are, how much traffic they take, how long your existing queries run, what your migration runner does around the file, whether a backfill in application code is batched, or whether the change is backwards compatible with the version of your app that is still running during a rolling deploy. A clean result means these checks found nothing; it is not a review of your migration.

    Does this connect to my database?

    No, and it has no way to. It reads SQL text and nothing else — no connection string, no credentials, no driver, no network calls at all. The browser page parses what you paste on your own device, and the CLI reads files from your own disk. That is what makes it safe to run against the migration you are about to apply to production: there is no connection to point at the wrong database.

    Which databases does this apply to?

    PostgreSQL. The lock levels, the rewrite rules, the NOT VALID / VALIDATE CONSTRAINT split and the CONCURRENTLY forms are all PostgreSQL semantics, and the advice would be wrong in places for MySQL, which has its own online-DDL rules, or SQLite, which rewrites tables for most ALTERs regardless. Running it against a MySQL migration will still flag statements that are risky there too, but read the reasoning rather than the verdict.

    More: why your migration locked the table. Already using squawk? See how this checker compares. Just reading the migration by eye? See how this checker compares for the relational checks a single-statement read tends to miss.

    No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not a database review, a performance audit, or a guarantee that a migration will not cause downtime or data loss, and it does not replace a qualified professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, including testing any suggested change against a copy of your own data before applying it to production. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

    Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, save check.mjs, engine.mjs and sql.mjs and run them yourself.

    Everything runs in your browser. The SQL you paste is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors, and the tool makes no network calls. Anonymous feature events (check_run, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

    A migration is one step in a deploy that can break quietly: Kubernetes Rollout Safety Check asks whether the rollout shipping this change drops requests, and Pinned Actions Check asks whether the workflow that ships it is pinned to immutable references — three slices of the same question.

    Slow queries are the other half of database trouble: Postgres EXPLAIN Analyzer reads an EXPLAIN ANALYZE plan and finds the missing index or disk spill.

    Free and open source. If this caught a migration that would have locked your table, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-reading-the-migration-by-hand.html.text:
SQL Migration Lock Check · comparison

SQL Migration Lock Check vs. reading the migration by hand

A careful reviewer genuinely catches the well-known single-statement case: a bare CREATE INDEX, a stray TRUNCATE. This page names no company or product — reading a migration file by hand before you run it is a habit most developers already have, not a competing tool.

What a careful read catches reliably

The risks that live entirely on one line are the ones a reviewer who knows the rules already catches well: CREATE INDEX with no CONCURRENTLY, VACUUM FULL, a bare TRUNCATE. This tool's create-index-not-concurrent, full-table-rewrite, and truncate checks flag exactly the same statements, for the same reason.

What gets harder as soon as it spans more than one line

CaseReading by handThis tool
A missing lock_timeoutDepends on whether a SET lock_timeout appears earlier in the same file, possibly dozens of lines away from the statement it protectsTracks every SET lock_timeout against every exclusive-lock statement below it, every time
NOT VALID + VALIDATE CONSTRAINT sharing one transactionBoth lines look correct individually; the bug is which BEGIN block they happen to sit insideFlags the pair specifically when they share a transaction, via validate-in-same-transaction
Several exclusive-lock statements in one transactionEach one reads as an acceptably brief lock on its own; adding five of them into one running total while reading top to bottom is easy to get wrongmany-locks-one-transaction reports the compounded hold, not each statement in isolation
ADD COLUMN with a volatile default, e.g. DEFAULT now()Looks identical to the cheap, metadata-only constant-default case Postgres 11+ made routine, unless the reader happens to know which functions are VOLATILEadd-column-volatile-default checks the function against Postgres's own volatility classification

The gap that matters most: a relationship between two statements, not a property of one

Whether an ALTER TABLE is protected by a lock_timeout, or whether a NOT VALID constraint's later VALIDATE actually buys a cheap step, is not visible on the risky line itself — it depends on what else the file does, sometimes many lines away. A reviewer has to hold the whole file's SET and transaction structure in mind while reading every later statement, which is the part that degrades fastest on a long or generated migration. This tool checks every statement against the full file's lock_timeout and transaction context the same way on every run, regardless of file length.

When to still read the migration yourself

This is a textual scan over SQL, not a query planner — it has no connection to your database, so it cannot see your table's actual row count, its column's current type, or whether an index it assumes exists actually does. It reports what a statement can do under Postgres's own locking rules, not a guarantee that it will hurt your specific table. Deciding whether a flagged statement is safe for your data, and catching SQL this tool's patterns don't recognise, is still a job for reading the migration yourself.

Common questions

What does reading a migration file by hand actually catch?

A reviewer who knows the rules catches the well-known single-statement case reliably: CREATE INDEX with no CONCURRENTLY, or a bare TRUNCATE. Those are real risks and a careful read finds them the same way this tool's create-index-not-concurrent and truncate checks do.

Why is a missing lock_timeout hard to catch by eye?

Whether a given ALTER TABLE is protected depends on whether a SET lock_timeout statement appears earlier in the same file -- a relationship between two statements that can be dozens of lines apart, not a property visible on the risky line itself. A reviewer has to hold the whole file's SET statements in mind while reading every ALTER, which is easy to get right on a short migration and easy to miss on a long generated one.

Why does NOT VALID plus VALIDATE CONSTRAINT in one transaction look safe when it is not?

Both statements are individually correct and idiomatic -- NOT VALID is the documented way to add a constraint without an immediate table scan. The trap is entirely about grouping: wrapped in the same BEGIN block as its own VALIDATE CONSTRAINT, the split buys nothing, because the transaction still holds the lock for the whole validation. Nothing about either line looks wrong on its own; the bug is which migration file boundary they happen to share.

Why is a run of several exclusive-lock statements easy to underestimate?

Each statement, read on its own, is an acceptably brief lock. Five of them in one transaction is not five brief locks -- it is one lock held from the first statement until the last one finishes, because Postgres does not release an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock until the transaction commits. Adding up five separate impact estimates in your head while reading a migration top to bottom is exactly the kind of running total a person is bad at keeping accurate.

Does this replace understanding what a flagged statement does?

No. This is a textual scan over SQL, not a query planner -- it cannot see your table's actual row count, current type, or whether an index already exists, so it reports what a statement can do under Postgres's locking rules, not a guarantee that it will hurt in your specific case. Deciding whether a flagged statement is actually safe for your table, and reading SQL this tool's patterns don't recognise, is still a job for reading the migration yourself.

Check a migration

It is not a database review or a guarantee that a migration will not cause downtime, and it does not replace a qualified professional. vs-squawk.html.text:
SQL Migration Lock Check · comparison

SQL Migration Lock Check vs. squawk

If you have searched for a PostgreSQL migration linter, you have found squawk. It is the established answer, and this page exists because pretending otherwise would waste your time. Here is what each tool is actually built to do — and, below, an explicit note on what this page is not.

What is the actual difference?

squawk parses SQL with a real PostgreSQL parser and reports per-statement rules, with editor and CI integration and a maintained rule set.

This checker scans statements textually, and its distinguishing checks are relational — about one statement in the context of another:

  • A missing lock_timeout. Whether an exclusive-lock statement is protected depends on whether a SET lock_timeout appears above it in the file. This is the check that matters most in practice, because it is the difference between a migration that fails harmlessly and one that stalls every query on the table.
  • NOT VALID and VALIDATE CONSTRAINT in one transaction. Both statements are individually correct and idiomatic. Together inside one BEGIN block they hold the lock for the whole validation anyway, so the two-step split — the entire point of writing it that way — buys nothing.
  • CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY inside a transaction block. Not a style problem: PostgreSQL refuses it outright at runtime. Since most migration frameworks wrap each file in a transaction by default, this is how a correct concurrency fix most often fails.
  • SET NOT NULL with a validated CHECK to lean on. On PostgreSQL 12+ this is either a cheap metadata change or a full table scan under an exclusive lock, and which one depends entirely on whether something earlier in the file added the constraint.

A per-statement rule engine cannot answer any of those from the statement alone. That is the wedge — not a claim that it finds more, but that these four are a different shape of question.

Side by side

SQL Migration Lock Checksquawk
InstallNone for the browser tool; three files and Node 18+ for the CLIA binary or package to install
ParsingTextual statement scanner (handles comments, dollar-quoting, transaction blocks)Real PostgreSQL parser
EmphasisRelational checks: lock queue exposure, transaction grouping, the fast pathsPer-statement rules across a broad, maintained set
Editor integrationNoYes
Runs in a browserYes — paste and read, nothing uploadedNo
Database accessNone, by constructionNone required

When is squawk the right answer?

When you want a maintained, widely-used linter with a real parser, editor integration, and a rule set more people have exercised than this one. A real parser is genuinely better than text scanning on unusual SQL — deeply nested expressions, exotic syntax, dialect edge cases — and if you are standardising migration linting across a team, established tooling with a community around it is worth more than any single clever check.

Install it. The two are not exclusive, and they disagree about very little. Use this one when you want an answer in ten seconds without installing anything, when you want the four relational checks above, or when the person who needs to understand the finding is not the person who set up the linter.

Is this a benchmark or a performance comparison?

No. Nothing here is measured against squawk — no rule-count comparison, no timing, no accuracy claim, and no run of squawk was performed to produce this page. It describes what each tool is built to do, based on each project's own stated purpose. If a specific claim on this page is out of date or wrong, it is a bug in this page.

Are you affiliated with squawk?

No. This project is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or connected to squawk or its maintainers in any way. squawk is named here because it is what a practitioner searching for this has probably already found.

why-your-migration-locked-the-table.html.text:
SQL Migration Lock Check · guide

Why your migration locked the table

The post-mortem that produced this page reads the same way every time: a one-line ALTER TABLE shipped on a Tuesday afternoon, the site returned errors for four minutes, and the statement itself ran in three milliseconds. Nobody was careless, and the migration was correct. What went wrong is a property of how PostgreSQL grants locks, and it is almost invisible until you have seen it once.

The statement ran in 3ms. Why was the site down for four minutes?

Because it spent those four minutes waiting to start, not running.

ALTER TABLE needs an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock — the strongest one, which conflicts with everything including the ACCESS SHARE that a plain SELECT holds. Your migration arrived while some long query was still reading the table, so it could not proceed and joined the lock queue. That much is expected and harmless.

The part that turns a wait into an outage is what happened behind it.

What is a lock queue and why does it block readers?

PostgreSQL grants table locks in request order, and it will not reorder them to let a compatible pair through. Two SELECTs can share a table happily — but if an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE request is sitting between them in the queue, the second SELECT waits behind it rather than joining the first.

This is deliberate. Without it, a steady stream of readers on a busy table would starve a writer forever. The consequence, though, is that one blocked DDL statement converts into a full table stall:

t=0     long analytics SELECT starts        (ACCESS SHARE, holds)
t=30s   ALTER TABLE arrives                 (ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, queued)
t=31s   ordinary SELECT arrives             (queued behind the ALTER)
t=32s   ordinary SELECT arrives             (queued)
        ... every request on this table now queues ...
t=4m    analytics SELECT finishes
t=4m    ALTER TABLE runs                    (3ms)
t=4m    the backlog drains

Between t=31s and t=4m the table was perfectly readable and nobody could read it. Your monitoring shows a latency cliff on one table, no slow query, and a migration that "took four minutes" — which sends the investigation at the migration, where there is nothing to find.

How does lock_timeout fix this?

It puts a bound on the waiting rather than on the work:

SET lock_timeout = '3s';
ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN ...;

Now PostgreSQL gives up if the lock is not available within three seconds, raising an error instead of queueing indefinitely. Nothing is blocked for longer than three seconds, the migration fails cleanly, and you retry — most retries succeed immediately, because the slow query has since finished.

Without it, the default is to wait forever. Which means the worst-case duration of your migration is the worst-case duration of any query on that table, a number you do not control and probably do not know.

Pair it with statement_timeout for the statements that do real work. They bound different things: lock_timeout bounds how long you wait to begin, statement_timeout bounds how long the work itself may take.

Which statements lock, and which actually rewrite the table?

Locking and rewriting are separate costs, and keeping them apart is most of what makes a migration reviewable. Everything in the first row is dangerous only because of the queue above; everything in the third holds the lock for minutes by design.

CostLockStatements
Metadata only — instant ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, briefly DROP COLUMN, RENAME, ADD COLUMN with a constant or STABLE default, DROP INDEX, attaching a pre-built index with USING INDEX
Full scan — reads every row ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, held throughout SET NOT NULL (without a validated CHECK), ADD CONSTRAINT / foreign key without NOT VALID
Full rewrite — writes every row ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, held throughout ALTER COLUMN TYPE, ADD COLUMN with a VOLATILE default (gen_random_uuid(), random()), VACUUM FULL, CLUSTER
Index build — blocks writes only SHARE CREATE INDEX without CONCURRENTLY

That last row is the one that gets missed. A SHARE lock lets reads through, so a health check that issues a SELECT keeps passing while every write to the table hangs. The symptom reaches you as connection-pool exhaustion or request timeouts, with nothing anywhere mentioning an index.

Two of these have exact fast paths worth memorising. ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT has been metadata-only since PostgreSQL 11 unless the default is volatile — so DEFAULT now() is free and DEFAULT gen_random_uuid() rewrites the table, from statements that look the same at a glance. And SET NOT NULL skips its scan on PostgreSQL 12+ if a validated CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) already proves the fact, which turns a locked scan into three cheap steps:

ALTER TABLE users ADD CONSTRAINT users_email_nn
  CHECK (email IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID;      -- instant

ALTER TABLE users VALIDATE CONSTRAINT users_email_nn;
                    -- scans, but under SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE:
                    -- reads and writes continue

ALTER TABLE users ALTER COLUMN email SET NOT NULL;
                    -- finds its proof, skips the scan

The VALIDATE step has to be in its own transaction. Inside one transaction no lock is released until commit, so doing both in a BEGIN block holds the table for the whole validation and buys you nothing at all.

Why did my CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY fail?

Almost certainly because it ran inside a transaction block, which PostgreSQL does not allow:

ERROR:  CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block

Most migration frameworks wrap each migration file in a transaction by default, so the correct fix gets rejected by the tooling that was trying to help. You have to opt out per migration — disable_ddl_transaction! in Rails, atomic = False in Django, -x in golang-migrate, an autocommit block in Alembic.

The second thing to know is that a failed concurrent build leaves an INVALID index behind. It takes space, it is not used for queries, and it must be dropped before you retry:

SELECT indexrelid::regclass FROM pg_index WHERE NOT indisvalid;

Checking a migration before you run it

Every pattern above is visible in the SQL text, which means it can be checked in a pull request rather than discovered in production. That is what this tool does — paste a migration, or wire the CLI into CI with --fail-on-risk. It reads the file and nothing else: no connection string, no credentials, no network calls.

Check a migration

This is general information about PostgreSQL behaviour, not advice about your database, and it does not replace a qualified professional. Lock behaviour and fast paths vary by PostgreSQL version — verify against the version you actually run, on a copy of your data, before relying on any of it.
